claims.text: Progressive creep deformation in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers is governed by the interfaces between the layers.
Compositional complexity and associated lattice distortion enhance local short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces.
FCC/BCC interfaces are preferential sites for dislocation nucleation.
Dislocations accumulate at FCC/BCC interfaces during sustained loading.
Evolving local order at the interfaces modifies local stress fields.
Interface-order-induced changes in stress fields promote strain localization and thereby drive creep.
The starting multilayer has pre-existing short-range order at its FCC/BCC interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion can promote dislocation nucleation.
High lattice friction associated with the complex interface structure impedes dislocation glide within the layers.
Local short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces impedes dislocation glide within the layers.
Interface-nucleated dislocations build up over time under sustained loading.
Cooperative dislocation motion can occur in compositionally complex HEAs.
The accumulation and cooperative motion of interface-nucleated dislocations produce localized plasticity and progressive creep strain.
Enhanced interfacial short-range order will increase the density of dislocations initiating at interfaces relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Enhanced interfacial short-range order will increase incremental creep strain under otherwise identical loading conditions.
Reducing interfacial short-range order will decrease the creep rate relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Reducing interfacial short-range order will decrease dislocation nucleation activity relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The proposed mechanism is limited to stresses and temperatures at which the multilayer structure is retained and neither catastrophic layer failure nor phase transformation occurs.
